title: Generic-fibre lifting and codimension for regular specializations
statement:
Let $r:P\to X$ be a regular morphism between Noetherian excellent schemes [def-exc-excellent-ring]; regular means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] with fibres that remain regular after every finite residue-field extension [def-weil-regular-scheme, def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Geometric points and their specializations are understood through maps of strict localizations [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. For a geometric specialization $v\rightsquigarrow w$ on a scheme $T$, let $c_T(v,w)$ be the Krull dimension of the reduced closure of $v$ in $T_{(w)}$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. A point is fibre-generic if its underlying point has codimension zero in its fibre. Put $b(t)=\dim\mathcal O_{P_{r(t)},t}$. For every geometric specialization $t'\rightsquigarrow t$ above $x'\rightsquigarrow x$ there are fibre-generic geometric points $\eta'$ over $x'$ and $\eta$ over $x$, with specializations $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta$, $\eta'\rightsquigarrow t'$ and $\eta\rightsquigarrow t$. The two composites $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta\rightsquigarrow t$ and $\eta'\rightsquigarrow t'\rightsquigarrow t$ agree, giving a commutative square. The vertical arrows $\eta'\rightsquigarrow t'$ and $\eta\rightsquigarrow t$ lie in the respective fibres. Given fibre-generic $\eta$ and $x'\rightsquigarrow x$, the fibre-generic lift $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta$ is unique up to a not necessarily unique isomorphism, and has codimension $c_X(x',x)$. A factorization of $x'\rightsquigarrow x$ into immediate specializations lifts to a factorization of $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta$ into immediate specializations through fibre-generic points. Moreover,
$$c_P(t',t)=c_X(x',x)+b(t)-b(t').$$
In particular the vertical arrows in the square have codimensions $b(t')$ and $b(t)$. Identity specializations and codimension-zero geometric isomorphisms are allowed.

source.place: Expose XVII, Lemmas 4.3.2.3–4.3.2.6; Expose XIV, Proposition 2.5.4. The codimension identity is the equality of lengths along the two paths of the square, using catenarity of the excellent strict local schemes.

proof.text:
Fix the specified target point $t$ and work with the induced map $P_{(t)}\to X_{(x)}$. By [lem-per-regular-strict-local-model] this is a regular map of excellent Noetherian strictly local schemes, and the fibre local dimensions at its points are the original $b(u)$. By [lem-per-local-dimension-function-calculus], choose a dimension function $\delta_X$ on $X_{(x)}$. By [lem-per-regular-dimension-function-pullback], $\delta_P(u)=\delta_X(r(u))-b(u)$ is a dimension function on $P_{(t)}$. The difference formula of [lem-per-local-dimension-function-calculus], applied on both schemes, now gives, for any geometric arrow $u\rightsquigarrow v$ in this setting,
$$c_P(u,v)=\delta_P(u)-\delta_P(v)=c_X(r(u),r(v))+b(v)-b(u).$$
Here codimensions are computed in the strict localizations belonging to these specified arrows, as in the statement.

source.place: XIV, Theorem 2.2.1 and Proposition 2.5.4; XVII, strict-local reduction in 4.3.2.4.

proof.text: For a fibre-generic geometric point $\eta$ over $x$, apply the strict-local reduction of Step 1 with $t=\eta$ and then [lem-per-strict-local-regular-integral-fibres]. The geometric fibre of $P_{(\eta)}\to X_{(x)}$ above the specified $x'$ is nonempty and integral, hence has one generic point. A geometric point over that generic point is a geometric specialization to the closed point $\eta$ lying over the specified base arrow. Its fibre local dimension is zero, so it is fibre-generic in $P$. Any fibre-generic lift must lie over that same generic point of this fibre. Choosing separable closures identifies its strict localization with the one just chosen, up to an isomorphism; such an isomorphism need not be unique. Thus the lift is unique in the geometric-specialization category in exactly the sense of the statement. We use geometric points through their strict localizations, not isomorphisms between arbitrary algebraically closed overfields.

source.place: XVII, proof of Lemma 4.3.2.4 from Lemma 4.3.2.3, printed p.285.

proof.text: Apply the formula of Step 1 after strict localization at this $\eta$. The two endpoints $\eta'$ and $\eta$ of the generic lift have $b=0$ by fibre-genericity. Therefore $c_P(\eta',\eta)=c_X(x',x)$. In particular a lift of a codimension-one base arrow has codimension one. If the base arrow is an identity or a geometric isomorphism, its lift has codimension zero.

source.place: XVII, final sentence of Lemma 4.3.2.4; XIV, Proposition 2.5.4.

proof.text: Given a finite factorization $x'=x_0\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow x_n=x$ into immediate arrows and the chosen endpoint $\eta_n=\eta$, construct $\eta_i\rightsquigarrow\eta_{i+1}$ backwards, from $i=n-1$ to $i=0$, by Step 2. Every $\eta_i$ is fibre-generic and every arrow has codimension one by Step 3, hence is immediate. The composite is a fibre-generic lift of the prescribed whole base arrow. Uniqueness in Step 2 identifies it, up to isomorphism at its source, with the originally specified $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta$; use this identification for the first endpoint. This is the required factorization of that arrow. The empty factorization gives the identity case.

source.place: XVII, proof of Lemma 4.3.2.5, printed p.285.

proof.text: To construct the square for $t'\rightsquigarrow t$, work in $P_{(t)}\to X_{(x)}$ with the specified arrows. By [lem-per-strict-local-regular-integral-fibres] the geometric fibre over $x$ is integral. Choose a geometric generic point $\eta$ of it and the resulting specialization $\eta\rightsquigarrow t$. Step 2 lifts $x'\rightsquigarrow x$ to $\eta'\rightsquigarrow\eta$. The specified $t'$ is a point of the geometric fibre of $P_{(t)}$ over $x'$, which is also integral by the cited node. Its generic point therefore specializes to $t'$. Choose a geometric representative $\eta''\rightsquigarrow t'$ of this specialization. The fibre-generic points $\eta'$ and $\eta''$ lie over the same generic point of this integral fibre, so identify their strict localizations by an isomorphism over that fibre. Compose it with $\eta''\rightsquigarrow t'$ to obtain the left vertical arrow. All these maps are over $P_{(t)}$; their maps to its closed geometric point $t$ are the specified structural maps. Hence their two composites to $t$ agree as geometric specializations. The vertical arrows lie over $x'$ and $x$, respectively, and both upper points are fibre-generic.

source.place: XVII, proof of Lemma 4.3.2.6, printed p.285.

proof.text: For the left vertical arrow the base arrow is the identity at $x'$, so Step 1 gives $c_P(\eta',t')=0+b(t')-0=b(t')$. Likewise $c_P(\eta,t)=b(t)$. Applied to the given bottom arrow, Step 1 gives exactly $c_P(t',t)=c_X(x',x)+b(t)-b(t')$. This also checks additivity along both paths: each path sum is $c_X(x',x)+b(t)$, the codimension of the common composite by Step 1. All differences are integers; equal endpoints and codimension-zero geometric isomorphisms yield zero and satisfy the same calculations.

proof_origin.place: XVII, proofs of Lemmas 4.3.2.4–4.3.2.6, using Lemma 4.3.2.3; XIV, Theorem 2.2.1 and Proposition 2.5.4.

Small cases agree: identity; generic to closed point of a smooth curve, 1=0+1−0; A¹ over a DVR, 2=1+1−0 and 1=1+1−1. No fixes, no tool_uses.
